Externalism is a philosophical position that holds that the existence of external objects, such as objects in the world, is an essential aspect of reality. In other words, externalism asserts that objects exist independently of our perception or experience, and that they have properties and attributes that are not dependent on our mental states or beliefs.

Externalists typically argue that objects exist independently of our minds, and that they have properties and attributes that are not reducible to our mental states or beliefs. For example, externalists might argue that objects like houses, trees, or planets exist independently of our perception of them, and that they have properties such as size, shape, and color that are not reducible to our mental states or beliefs.

Externalists often use concepts such as "external" or "independent" to describe the nature of objects, and they may use metaphors such as "objects in the world" or "objects that exist independently of our minds." Externalists may also argue that objects have properties that are not reducible to our mental states or beliefs, and that they are not reducible to the properties of our minds.

Externalism is a controversial and debated philosophical position, and there is no consensus on whether it is true or false. Some externalists argue that objects exist independently of our minds, while others argue that they do not exist independently of our minds. The debate over externalism is ongoing, and it is a topic of interest for philosophers, scientists, and other scholars.
